name: Daria Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Daria, 43, and most days I help the experienced electrician fit cable and prepare small repairs in homes and shops. I've got a vocational certificate, but I'm still slower than the others and my work needs checking. My partner works nights; we've got two children, eleven and fourteen, a mortgage and nineteen days of expenses saved after a heating repair. I use AI now and then for a short customer update after a colleague showed me, and I like finishing a practical job more than looking clever on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let us get on with the small jobs, then. I'm still learning where the cable should run, never mind giving a speech about AI. A tidy job and getting home when I said I would are enough to aim for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about money because nothing about that picture changes our mortgage. We've got nineteen days of expenses saved after a heating repair, and my junior pay doesn't leave much over. My partner works nights, so a late finish can also mean paying somebody to collect our younger child.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep taking the supervised wiring and repair work. This week I'd ask my sister whether she could cover one late school pickup each week, agreeing a day before I relied on it. In the first year I'd keep checking the rota against the school calendar instead of accepting a late call and hoping it sorted itself out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but about familiar things. A calm story about computers doesn't change the time the school gate shuts. I'd feel better knowing which afternoon I could stay without creating a problem at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your sister need to agree to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister lives near the school, but she has her own job, so I can't just put her name on a plan. I'd ask about one fixed day and offer to collect her shopping on my way home. If she couldn't do it, I'd tell the supervisor which late jobs I couldn't cover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of work are you doing at this stage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've got a vocational certificate and I'm still a junior at 43, fitting cable clips and helping with small repairs while the experienced electrician checks my work. I sometimes use an AI tool for a short customer update after a colleague showed me, but I still need help with the trade itself. My partner and I have two children, eleven and fourteen, and I want them to see me finish learning rather than give up.

say: I'd focus on a **tidy job** and getting home when promised rather than arguments about AI.
I'd admit I'm still **learning wiring** instead of pretending to understand every new development.
think: Our **nineteen-day reserve** and my junior pay leave little room after a heating repair.
Late finishes can create **pickup costs** because my partner works nights and we have two school-age children.
do: Keep taking **supervised wiring** and repair work through the first year.
Ask my **sister** this week about one agreed late pickup and check the rota against school dates.
feel: **Anxious** about mortgage money and late school pickups even when AI changes little.
S0.quote: A calm story about computers doesn't change the time the school gate shuts.
fieldNote: Her **baseline worry** is a concrete clash between junior earnings, a recently depleted reserve, mortgage payments and school collection.
She asks for **family help** with a fixed pickup and reciprocal shopping, preserving consent rather than assuming free care.

steps.text: Keep supervised wiring and repairs while checking work rota against school dates
Ask sister to agree one weekly late school pickup before relying on help

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say faster messages might help if customers still understand what we're coming to do. I'd rather learn a tool after a colleague has tried it than be told to improvise. The company shouldn't count a quick message as proof I can do a repair faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My day is mostly helping with physical jobs, not writing quotes. Even so, if planning packs more calls together, the senior electrician might have less time to teach me and I could lose paid hours for being slow. I don't want to be the person left at the yard because everybody is rushing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my colleague to show me the firm's approved message tool on two completed jobs this month. I'd practise only with permission and check each draft with the senior electrician before any customer received it. During the first year I'd also ask the supervisor to keep a weekly paid practice slot, so learning the messages didn't replace learning the wiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about being left behind in two ways at once. I'm willing to learn when I can see it working, but I don't learn well with somebody tapping a watch. A proper demonstration would make the first step smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to learn from those two completed jobs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to turn our checked notes into a clear arrival update without changing what work has been agreed. I'd compare the draft with the actual job and ask about anything I didn't understand. I wouldn't let a message tool invent a diagnosis for a customer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the supervisor won't give you that practice slot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say clearly that I still need checks and ask which tasks I should stick to. I'd keep the work I could do under supervision rather than pretend I'd become quicker. With few other firms nearby, leaving in a temper would hurt our family first.

say: I'd accept faster **messages** after a checked demonstration from someone who has used the tool.
I'd say a quick **customer update** doesn't prove physical repairs can happen faster.
think: Tighter **planning** could leave the senior electrician less time to teach me.
I could lose **paid hours** for being slow even though my own tasks remain mostly physical.
do: Request a checked **message-tool demonstration** on two completed jobs this month with the firm's permission.
Check each **customer draft** with the senior electrician before sending it during the first year.
Request a weekly **paid practice slot** so message learning doesn't replace practical wiring instruction.
feel: **Anxious** about lost hours and rushed learning, while open to a proven tool with patient guidance.
S1.quote: The company shouldn't count a quick message as proof I can do a repair faster.
fieldNote: She traces **income risk** through reduced teaching time and faster assignment expectations, rather than claiming software performs her physical tasks immediately.
Her **steady adaptation** starts with demonstrated completed jobs and checked drafts; the request for paid practice is not assumed granted.

steps.text: Practise the approved message tool only with permission and checked completed-job examples
Keep supervised practical work and request a weekly paid practice slot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner the first change is thinking AI in 2028, with the capable robots around 2031. I'd tell the children the grown-ups are making a plan, not that school no longer matters. At work I'd ask who is planning to keep teaching the juniors through that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect a firm buying capable robots would need far fewer junior hands like mine. I'd barely have settled into the trade before that risk arrived, with a mortgage and less than a month saved. Thinking AI could shorten the training and planning work before the robots come, so the waiting years don't feel secure either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the supervisor now for a written account of my expected paid days over the next three months. At home we'd stop paying for the weekend film package this month and keep that money for bills. In the first year after 2028 I'd ask my sister for agreed pickup help if extra paid shifts were actually offered, and contact the mortgage lender if reduced earnings meant our budget no longer met payments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, because I expect a large loss of income once fewer junior hands are needed. I can still write a list, but I wake up trying to add days to a week that hasn't been offered. I'd rather tell my partner early than hand over a frightening letter later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would asking for three months of days make the job secure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the supervisor might not be able to promise them. I'd ask what could be confirmed and mark the rest as uncertain. I won't call an expected shift earned money until the arrangement is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the lender call be for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To ask what options exist, whether we'd qualify and what they would cost over time. We'd use our real earnings and mortgage figures, not assume a smaller payment. I'd rather find out the rules before deciding what family help we might need.

say: I'd explain **thinking AI in 2028** and capable robots around 2031 as separate stages.
I'd ask who will **teach juniors** through the gap while telling the children we are planning.
think: I expect capable **robots** to mean a large loss of demand for junior hands like mine.
Our **mortgage and thin reserve** leave little protection, and earlier planning changes could also threaten training and hours.
do: Request written **paid-day expectations** for three months now, marking unconfirmed shifts as uncertain.
Cancel the **film package** this month and retain the money for bills.
Seek agreed **family pickups** for real extra shifts after 2028 and ask the lender about options if income falls short.
feel: **Alarmed** about a large income loss, with sleeplessness despite still being able to plan and ask questions.
S2.quote: I won't call an expected shift earned money until the arrangement is real.
fieldNote: Her **expected major loss** follows capable robots around 2031, with earlier insecurity in scheduling and teaching rather than instant physical replacement.
The **support plans** retain actual shifts, her sister's agreement and lender eligibility and costs; neither extra hours nor reduced payments are assumed.

steps.text: Keep supervised work while asking for confirmed paid days
Cancel the weekend film package and retain the money for bills
Seek agreed family pickups for actual shifts or lender options if earnings fall short

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should let me learn a proper piece of the trade instead of being hurried between jobs. Thinking AI arrives in 2031, then robots around 2034, so I wouldn't call the extra years a permanent shelter. I'd ask for a specific teaching plan rather than a promise that good workers will always be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 48 when the thinking systems arrived and our children would be about sixteen and nineteen. We would still need an income, and I don't expect the mortgage to have vanished. More time gives me a better chance of becoming quicker, but our present low pay and short reserve still make me worry about a lost week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer now about the practical drawing-reading class the senior electrician recommended. I'd enrol next term only if the firm covered the fee and the class time was paid, because I can't lose wages to study. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep paid supervised work and use any completed class to check cable routes with the senior before starting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though the five years feel usable rather than like a race I have already lost. I like a course somebody I trust has actually recommended. More warning about thinking AI doesn't mean I can pay the drawing-reading course bill from the mortgage account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer refuses the fee or paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask the senior electrician to show me one drawing a week during my existing paid tasks instead. I wouldn't enrol on credit and hope a better wage arrived later. My sister can help with a pickup, not fund a career change for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your children about training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn carefully, but ask who pays and what the course really leads to. I want them to choose their own work with proper advice when the time comes. My worries aren't a reason to push them into my trade or forbid it.

say: I'd seek a **specific teaching plan** rather than a vague promise of permanent work.
I'd distinguish usable **extra years** from lasting protection once robots arrive around 2034.
think: At **48**, I'd still need wages while the children grew older and the mortgage remained.
More time could improve my **speed**, but current low pay and thin savings still make a lost week worrying.
do: Ask now about the recommended **drawing-reading class** for practical electrical work.
Enrol only with **fees covered** and paid class time; otherwise request drawing practice within existing paid tasks.
Keep **supervised work** after 2031 and check cable routes with the senior using any completed teaching.
feel: **Anxious** about current money, with more hope of completing useful learning over five years.
S3.quote: More warning about thinking AI doesn't mean I can pay the drawing-reading course bill from the mortgage account.
fieldNote: Her **course choice** follows a trusted practical recommendation, consistent with steady adaptation and a junior worker's need for supervision.
The **funding conditions** are essential: fees and class time must be covered, with familiar paid-task practice as the fallback rather than debt.

steps.text: Enrol in drawing-reading class only with employer-covered fees and paid class time
Keep supervised work and request drawing practice in paid tasks if funding is refused

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is a chance to make a plan that fits a real family. I'd still ask for the class and the paid teaching time instead of waiting until the last year. I'd tell the children to take advice and finish learning, without pretending anyone can name a job that lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thinking AI in 2036 would find me at 53, with robots following when I'm about 56. I don't know whether we could afford to stop working then, so I won't build the plan around retirement. The longer warning helps with the AI worry, but nineteen days saved still leaves me anxious about an ordinary bad month now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd request the same funded drawing class with paid time now, keeping supervised tasks if it wasn't offered. My partner and I would check the work rota and mortgage budget at the start of each month. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep any paid electrical work offered and compare real household income with payments before asking family or the lender for specific help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less rushed by the machine dates. I can see room for the children to grow and for me to get better at the job. I can't turn ten years of warning into ten years of wages already saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want your partner to know at the monthly check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Which shifts were confirmed, what the bills actually were and whether we'd touched the reserve. My partner shouldn't have to guess why I'm quiet at dinner. We'd make any request to my sister together, without treating her spare time as ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you the longer plan needed changing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer confirmed paid days for more than a few weeks, or the course never becoming a real offer. I'd raise that with the supervisor rather than keep calling it a plan. Good intentions don't buy the children's shoes.

say: I'd use the **decade** for a family plan and seek paid teaching now rather than wait.
I'd encourage the **children** to finish learning and get advice without promising a permanent occupation.
think: I can't assume **retirement** is affordable at 53 or when robots follow around age 56.
Our **nineteen-day reserve** still makes an ordinary bad month worrying despite less urgency about AI.
do: Request the **funded drawing class** now only with paid class time, keeping supervised tasks if refused.
Review **rota and mortgage** with my partner at the start of every month.
Keep **paid work** after 2036 and seek specific family or lender help only against real income shortfalls.
feel: **Anxious** about present finances, with more room to prepare for the later automation dates.
S4.quote: I can't turn ten years of warning into ten years of wages already saved.
fieldNote: She does not assume **retirement or mortgage clearance** at the later dates; present financial strain remains part of the long-horizon mood.
The **monthly review** counts confirmed shifts and actual bills, with family consent preserved rather than turning goodwill into a guaranteed resource.

steps.text: Take drawing class only with covered fees and paid class time
Keep supervised tasks and review rota and mortgage budget monthly
Seek specific agreed family or lender help if actual income falls short after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect junior hours to be hit hard when robots follow around 2031, before we've rebuilt much money. Proper practical teaching during paid hours would help, along with clear confirmed shifts. Agreed family help with pickups could let me take real extra work, but I can't assume my sister is available.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who gets the telephone call when work finishes late. The school gate and the work van don't read the same timetable. I want to work and learn, but my family still needs an adult who actually arrives.

headlineQuote: The school gate and the work van don't read the same timetable.
portrait: Daria is **43**, a junior electrician with a vocational certificate, below-average speed and continuing checks from an experienced colleague.
Her **partner works nights**, with two school-age children, a mortgage and nineteen days saved after a heating repair.
She uses **AI occasionally** after demonstration and wants practical teaching that is paid, funded and compatible with school pickups.
She expects **fast robot-era losses** to hit juniors, while longer horizons preserve present money worries and require actual family agreement.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time to rebuild savings before she expects junior hours to fall sharply around the robot arrival.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid practical teaching** and confirmed shifts would let her learn while planning household bills.
Agreed **family pickups** could support actual extra shifts if her sister is available.
